Dear Ricky,
It was a real pleasure to meet you, and great to be introduced through David.
Key Points from Our Meeting:
- Your Situation and Goals: You have decided to retire now, brought forward from your original plan due to changes at work. Your primary goal is simple: remove money worries, take some lump sums from your pensions, and have a reliable income that covers your day-to-day needs without stress. I want to reassure you that based on what we have discussed, you are going to be okay. Once I have built the cash flow model and shown you the full picture, I am confident you will see that clearly.
- Your Financial Position: You own your home at 56 Adelaide Gardens, mortgage-free, with an estimated value of around £510,000 ( I checked the latest valuation online).  You have cash savings of approximately £100,000, including around £40,000 from your wife's life insurance payout. Please do confirm the precise figure when you get a chance. Other than your pensions, there are no other significant assets.
- Your Pensions: You have four pension arrangements. The Tower Hamlets defined benefit scheme is the most significant: it provides a guaranteed income and is not transferable, so you must choose one of the options on offer. The current figures show an annual pension of around £13,278 with a lump sum of £39,000, though other commutation options are available. I will analyse these in detail and advise you on which option makes the most sense for your circumstances. The remaining three are money purchase pots: The People's Pension valued at under £10,000, a Standard Life pension of approximately £45,000, and a Mears Group workplace pension of approximately £45,000. The plan is to consolidate these three into a single arrangement to simplify everything and invest them in a clear, consistent strategy. There is also what you believe may be an ISA, previously with Virgin Money and now with Octopus, worth around £10,000. Please send me the paperwork on that so I can confirm what it is.
- Retirement Income: Your Tower Hamlets pension and your State Pension together will provide approximately £2,000 per month, which broadly covers your estimated monthly expenditure. Your State Pension of around £12,500 per year is payable from age 67, which is four years away. In the meantime, we will use your cash savings and pension capital to bridge that gap, keeping your money working efficiently rather than drawing it down unnecessarily.
- Tax Planning Opportunity: Before you retire, there is a worthwhile planning exercise to consider. In the current tax year, you could make a pension contribution of up to around £39,000. By contributing approximately £31,000 net, that immediately becomes £39,000 in your pension through tax relief, representing a gain of around £8,000. Even if retiring a month or two later allowed a larger contribution, I would not want this to hold you back if you are ready to go sooner. We will work around your preferred retirement date and make the most of what is available.
- Estate Planning and Beneficiaries: Your pension beneficiary nominations are currently out of date following your wife's passing and need to be updated across all four pensions to name your sons, Ricky Joe and Ronnie. I am pleased to hear you are in the process of arranging a will and a Lasting Power of Attorney through the company David referred you to. Please do prioritise getting both completed. Your estate is estimated at around £800,000, and because you inherited your wife's nil-rate band on her death, that estate would likely pass to your boys free of inheritance tax. If you also wanted to make provision for your two granddaughters, that is something to discuss with the solicitor when you sit down to draught the will.
- State Pension Forecast: You have not yet requested a State Pension forecast but given that you have worked continuously since leaving school, you are almost certainly entitled to the full amount. Please log on to the HMRC gateway, or ask one of your boys to help you, and request a forecast to confirm there are no gaps in your National Insurance record.
Next Steps:
1. Documents to send me: Please send over a photograph of your most recent payslip or P60, your driving licence for identification purposes, and a copy of the most up-to-date letters for each pension, particularly the latest Standard Life letter. Also send me whatever paperwork you have for the Octopus account so I can confirm whether it is an ISA.
2. Cash savings: Please confirm the precise total across all your accounts. This is important for the cash flow model.
3. State Pension forecast: Please log on to the HMRC gateway and request your State Pension forecast. If you get stuck, let me know and I will point you in the right direction.
4. Will and Lasting Power of Attorney: Please progress both as a priority with the company you have been referred to. The LPA is important, as it ensures a trusted person can manage your affairs if ever needed.
5. Beneficiary nominations: Once we have consolidated the money purchase pensions, we will update the nominations across all arrangements to name your sons.
6. Cash flow model and follow-up meeting: Once I have received the documents and the letters of authority responses come back from the providers, I will build your full cash flow model, and we will arrange a second meeting to go through the plan together. That should be around four to six weeks from now. At that meeting, you will see your full financial picture set out clearly, including the retirement income projections, the pension consolidation plan, the Tower Hamlets options analysis, and the pre-retirement contribution opportunity.
The overall picture is a reassuring one. You have a mortgage-free home, meaningful savings, a guaranteed pension from Tower Hamlets, and a State Pension to follow in four years. The priorities now are getting the documents across to me, confirming your savings figure, and progressing the will and Lasting Power of Attorney. Everything else follows from there.
I very much look forward to speaking again soon, and to showing you the full picture at our next meeting.
Best wishes,
Jim

Dear Jason,
It was a pleasure to meet you today, and thank you for bringing in all your paperwork. I hope you are feeling better after your recent illness. Below is a summary of what we discussed and what happens next.
Your goals
Your priority is to consolidate your pensions, consolidate the tax-free cash, and use it to clear your outstanding debts. You were clear that you want to get your head above water financially, and everything we discussed was framed around that.
Your pensions
Your five pensions have a combined value of approximately £334,000.

 Money purchase (Scottish Widows,      Aviva, Standard Life): these are straightforward and can be      consolidated into a SIPP without complication.
 Defined benefit (Ford and Alstom): these      need a more involved process, explained below. Their combined transfer      value is approximately £170,000, and the Ford scheme alone is promising a      pension of around £4,400 a year.

Defined benefit transfers
The regulatory starting position is that you should not transfer a defined benefit pension, because you would be giving up a guaranteed income for life. A pension transfer specialist must therefore assess both schemes, interview you to confirm you understand what you would be giving up, and provide written advice. Their conclusion will almost certainly be to keep the pensions. You are entitled to go against that advice and proceed as an insistent client, which you have told me is your intention.
The specialist firm I will introduce you to is PensionWorks. Their fee is likely to be £5,000 to £6,000, and it is paid from your pension fund rather than from your own pocket.
Tax-free cash and clearing your debts
Once all five pensions are consolidated, you can take 25% of the fund as tax-free cash, approximately £83,000. That is more than enough to clear your current debts of around £60,000:

 second      charge on your home: approximately £42,000
 Ecotricity:      an estimated £10,000
 HMRC:      approximately £6,000
 Santander:      the remaining balance

What remains invested
After taking the tax-free cash, you would have a residual fund of approximately £250,000. I strongly encourage you to leave it invested for growth until you formally retire, which at the expected retirement age of 67 is around 10 to 12 years away.
Investment approach
We invest in a slice of the entire global stock market rather than picking individual stocks or trying to second-guess markets. Our 80/20 strategy has delivered annualised returns of around 10% since 1985. Please remember that past performance is not a reliable guide to future returns, that the value of investments can fall as well as rise, and that you may get back less than you invest. The key discipline is to stay invested and not react to short-term market movements.
Two financial plans
At our next meeting I will show two plans side by side: your current position with your debts in place, and the outcome after consolidating the pensions, taking the tax-free cash and clearing the debts. This will let you see the difference the plan makes and make a fully informed decision.
Joanne's pensions and the State Pension
Joanne has frozen pensions with Royal London from her time at the solicitor's firm. We need their values for the plan, and a pension search may be worth doing to confirm there are no others. You and Joanne will both qualify for the State Pension at 67. Please check your National Insurance records through the HMRC government gateway so we can include your projected entitlement.
Wills and Lasting Powers of Attorney
You confirmed you want both in place. They are important, so please do not let this drift. We will return to them once the pension work is under way.
Our fees

 Initial      fee: 1’5% of assets for the money purchase consolidation and 1.5% for the      defined benefit transfer work.
 Ongoing      advice fee: 0.75% a year.
 All      fees are taken from your funds rather than paid directly by you.

Next steps
Complete your fact-find and expenses online (the most important step). Please use this secure link to enter your and Joanne's details, including income, regular outgoings, and the balance and interest rate of each debt: https://api.plannrcrm.com/fact... Please be as accurate as you can, as this drives the financial plan. Include anything you know about Joanne's pensions.
2. Letters of authority. I will send the six signed letters to your pension providers to request up-to-date valuations and transfer terms. Providers typically take two to three weeks to respond.
3. Joanne's Royal London pensions. Please send me any paperwork you have for these.
4. State Pension forecasts. Please share forecasts for both you and Joanne from the HMRC government gateway.
5. Follow-up meeting. Once I have the valuations and you have completed the online fact-find, I will invite you and Joanne in to go through the two plans. We are aiming for early to mid-November, depending on how quickly the providers respond.
6. PensionWorks introduction. If, after seeing the numbers, you confirm you want to proceed with the defined benefit transfers, I will introduce you to PensionWorks.

The overall picture is one that can genuinely be turned around. The pension values are meaningful and the tax-free cash will comfortably clear what you owe. The priority now is to complete the online fact-find and expenses so I can build your plan. Everything else follows from there.
Please get in touch at any point if you have questions.

[circle note by Jim Hoban on 2026-10-13]
Following our discussion about taking your full pension benefits from Nucleus, I need to explain two points that must be dealt with before we go ahead.

1. Your tax code and the "emergency tax code"
Because you have never taken benefits from this pension, Nucleus have confirmed they hold no tax code for you from HMRC. Where this is the case, the pension provider is required to apply an emergency tax code to the first payment.
An emergency tax code treats the payment as though you will receive that same amount every month for the rest of the tax year. Your personal allowance and tax bands are applied to just one month's worth of income, rather than to the whole year. On a large one-off withdrawal, this means far more tax is deducted at source than you will ultimately owe. You can reclaim the overpayment from HMRC afterwards, but this can take several weeks and would leave you temporarily out of pocket by a significant amount.
2. How we can avoid this
There are two ways to deal with it:
- My recommendation is that you contact HMRC directly first, explain that you are about to take a large pension payment from Nucleus and that no tax code is held, and ask them to resolve your tax code so that it can be confirmed to Nucleus before the full payment is made. The Income Tax helpline details are here: https://www.gov.uk/find-hmrc-c... (from outside the UK: +44 135 535 9022).
- Alternatively, we can take a small initial payment of around £5,000 from your pension through income drawdown. This triggers the process, and HMRC will then issue the correct tax code to Nucleus. The small payment would be taxed on the emergency basis, but any overpayment on it is minor and reclaimable. Once the correct code is in place, we can then take the remainder.
Please let me know how you would like to proceed. If you do speak to HMRC, please tell me what they say so that I can liaise with Nucleus.
3. Bank account verification
Nucleus currently have no bank account on file for you, so they cannot pay out until one has been verified. Could you please send me a recent bank statement (ideally dated within the last three months) for the account you would like the money paid into? It needs to show your name, the account number and sort code. I will upload it to Nucleus to verify the account and update your records.
If you have any questions on any of this, please call me.
Kind regards,
Jim

Key Points from Our Meeting:
- Christopher's Passing: Margaret, you updated us on Christopher's passing and the circumstances surrounding his final days. The medical examiner's office has now confirmed the cause of death, which means you are able to obtain the death certificate and proceed with registering his death and organising the funeral. We are thinking of you and Hella throughout all of this.
- Immediate Next Steps on the Estate: Once the death certificate is in hand, the next step is to register Christopher's death and then apply for a Grant of Probate. As Christopher's will leaves everything to you, provided you survive him by 30 days, the process should be relatively straightforward. The will is held by a firm in Croydon, and you confirmed you know how to access it. Anything held in Christopher's sole name, including bank accounts and the Walthamstow property, will require the Grant of Probate before you can deal with them. Anything in joint names passes to you directly.
- Christopher's Financial Position: Having gone through Christopher's papers, his liquid assets across cash and investment accounts total approximately £603,000, minus the £37,000 ISA already transferred, and the £50,000 in National Savings, giving approximately £516,000 in cash and investments. In addition, there is a likely death-in-service lump sum from his final salary pension of approximately £125,000. Total liquid assets are therefore approximately £900,000. The Walthamstow property is valued at approximately £750,000, giving a total potential liquidity of around £1.65 million once the tenancy is resolved.
- Capital Gains Tax on the Walthamstow Property: An important point to note is that on Christopher's death, the Capital Gains Tax that had previously accrued on the Walthamstow property is extinguished. The property passes to you at its current market value, meaning that if you were to sell it, there would be no Capital Gains Tax liability arising from Christopher's period of ownership.
- The Walthamstow Property: You were clear that you do not wish to continue as a landlord. The options we discussed are selling the property, retaining it and doing it up with a view to gifting or lending it to Hella, or selling it and helping Hella buy elsewhere. Each comes with different cost and tax implications, and there is no need to rush this decision. I will look into the process for formally ending the tenancy when you are ready to proceed.
- Inheritance Tax and the Estate: The total estate, including both properties and all liquid assets, is currently valued at approximately £2.8 million, giving rise to an estimated Inheritance Tax liability of around £600,000. A three-pronged strategy was outlined: strategic gifting, investing into trust structures, and potentially a life insurance policy to underpin any remaining liability. There is no immediate action required, but this will form the backbone of the financial plan we build together in due course.
- Deed of Variation: Jim introduced the concept of a Deed of Variation on Christopher's will. You have two years from the date of his death to make changes, and this mechanism could allow Christopher's Nil-Rate Band of £325,000, and potentially the Residence Nil-Rate Band bringing it to £500,000, to be used for tax-efficient gifting from his estate. This could form the first stage of a longer-term gifting strategy. No decisions are needed now, but it is worth keeping in mind.
- Trusts and Protecting Hella: Rather than making outright gifts to Hella, Jim introduced the idea of placing assets into a trust of which Hella is the beneficiary and you are the trustee. The trust could make a loan to Hella to help her onto the property ladder, while keeping you in control and protecting the assets from any future third-party claims. This is the approach Jim would encourage over outright gifting at this stage, particularly given Hella's age and her circumstances. Once you are satisfied the time is right, the loan can be waived.
- Assisting Mary: You mentioned that your sister Mary is actively looking to purchase a property and is considering a mortgage of around £550,000. You would like to help her. The options discussed were an outright gift or an interest-free loan, with the loan remaining an asset in your estate but waivable on death through your will. Jim suggested the best next step is a joint meeting with you and Mary so that we can understand the full picture and advise properly. There is no urgency: Mary should find a property first, and your ability to help will simply inform the ceiling of what she considers.
- Gifting Out of Regular Income: Katie confirmed that regular gifts made from surplus income, provided they do not impact your standard of living and are demonstrably regular, fall immediately outside your estate and are not subject to the seven-year rule. This could be a straightforward way to provide Hella with a regular allowance without any Inheritance Tax concerns, and can start at any level that feels comfortable.
- Your Will and Lasting Power of Attorney: Your current will and financial Lasting Power of Attorney both name Hella as sole executor and attorney. Jim's advice is to consider adding a second person to both documents in case anything were to happen to Hella. Your will should also be reviewed once you have determined your gifting intentions, so that it reflects what you actually want to pass on at that point. There is no rush, but it is on the list.
Next Steps:
1. Death Certificate and Registration: Please obtain the death certificate and register Christopher's death as soon as you are able. This is the key step that unlocks everything else.
2. Grant of Probate: Once the death certificate is in hand, Jim will help guide you through the Grant of Probate process and will recommend a solicitor to assist you. You do not need to do this alone.
3. Walthamstow Property and Tenancy: Once you have decided on the direction of travel for the property,  Jim will investigate the formal process for ending the tenancy. In the meantime, the council will be able to advise you on the existing tenancy arrangement, as the rent is paid through them.

5. Meeting with Mary: Please arrange for a follow-up meeting in due course with both you and Mary present, so that we can understand her financial position and advise properly on how best you can assist her with her property purchase.
6. Your Will and LPA: Please give some thought to who you would like to add as a second executor and attorney alongside Hella. We would recommend involving a solicitor to update both documents once your gifting plans are clearer.
7. Follow-Up Planning Meeting: Once things have settled and the Grant of Probate is underway, we will arrange a follow-up meeting to build your full financial and estate plan. This will cover the gifting strategy, trust structures, investment of the liquid assets, and the insurance question. There is no rush. Take your time.
The overall picture, when you are ready to look at it, is a strong one. Christopher clearly worked hard and quietly throughout his life, and you are in a position of real financial security. The priorities now are the death certificate, registering his passing, and allowing yourself the time and space to grieve. Everything financial will wait. We are here whenever you need us.
Please do not hesitate to reach out at any point, whether it is a question or just to talk something through.
Best wishes,

1. It is not a UK registered pension. The Brock is approved and regulated in Guernsey rather than registered with HMRC, and most UK providers will only accept transfers from UK registered schemes, or at most from approved overseas transfer schemes (QROPS), which the Brock has never been.
2. Its tax position would be unclear in the UK. You have already taken your tax-free cash and are drawing income under Guernsey rules. These do not fit neatly into UK pension categories, and if a provider classified the money wrongly it could face tax charges itself. Most would rather not take that risk.
3. The checks involved are complex. Accepting the plan would mean checking an overseas trust, an offshore investment bond and structured products, and tracing the original source of the money back to your earlier Guernsey scheme. For mainstream providers that is more work and risk than they are prepared to take on.
My recommended approach
I have set out my recommendation in the attached file note. In summary:
- Stay with Sovereign and RL360 for now. Leaving today would mean paying RL360's early exit charge, currently around £20,000. This charge reduces every quarter and ends in February 2032, so I suggest we look again at moving the plan at that point.

1. IHT position on your death
From 6 April 2027, pension funds — including your SSAS — will form part of your taxable estate for Inheritance Tax for the first time. This is a significant change; historically pensions have sat outside the estate.
Based on current asset values (SSAS c.£550,000, main residence c.£200,000, ISA/GIA c.£300,000 — total c.£1.05m), and taking into account your planned gift of £150,000 to help with a grandson's property purchase around his wedding, our current estimate is that the potential IHT liability on your death ranges from nil up to c.£219,000, depending on:
- Confirmation of how much of your late wife's Nil Rate Band and Residence Nil Rate Band remains transferable to you, given the discretionary trust arrangement in her Will
- Whether you survive at least 7 years from the date of the £150,000 gift
- The residence passing to a direct descendant to secure the Residence Nil Rate Band
I want to stress this is a range, not a confirmed figure — we need several pieces of information from your Marie’s estate and some decisions from you before I can narrow it down. These are set out below.
2. A separate issue: funding any tax due from the SSAS
A large part of the SSAS value is held in commercial property rather than cash. If IHT becomes due on your pension value after April 2027, this needs to be settled by your personal representatives — but property isn't a liquid asset. Under the new rules, personal representatives can ask the scheme to withhold up to 50% of the death benefit for up to 15 months to help fund the tax, but that doesn't solve the underlying problem if the SSAS itself doesn't hold enough cash. [task note by Jim Hoban on 2026-08-11 "HMRC Tax Demand"]
Dear Alex,
Following the letter you've received from HMRC, I wanted to set out (1) the tax position on the Momentum bond and (2) the steps you need to take to respond to HMRC.
1. The tax position on your Momentum bond
The bond was set up in September 2019 with a total investment of £130,000. Based on the information HMRC has received from Momentum via the exchange of information with Guernsey, the gross proceeds on encashment were £146,540.98.
On that basis, the chargeable gain is:
Gross proceeds: £146,540.98
Less original investment: £130,000.00
Chargeable event gain: £16,540.98 
As this is an offshore bond, the whole of this gain is added to your income for the tax year of encashment and taxed at your marginal rate(s). Unlike a UK bond, there is no 20% notional tax credit already deemed paid within the bond, so the full gain is taxable - there's no basic-rate offset.
With your salary of £90,000, you're already a higher-rate (40%) taxpayer. Adding the gain of £16,540.98 takes total income for the year to around £106,541, which:
- keeps the gain within the 40% band (it doesn't reach the £125,140 additional-rate threshold), but
- because total income exceeds £100,000, your personal allowance would start to taper away (£1 lost for every £2 over £100,000) if the gain were simply added in full.
This is exactly the situation top-slicing relief exists to address. It spreads the gain over the number of complete years the bond has been held (c. 5 years, from September 2019) to work out an "annual slice", calculates tax on that slice, and compares it to a straight calculation on the full gain to establish the relief due.
On the figures we have:
- Annual slice: £16,540.98 ÷ 5 = £3,308.20
- Adding this slice to your £90,000 income keeps you comfortably under £100,000, so no personal allowance taper applies at the sliced level
- Tax on the slice: £3,308.20 x 40% = £1,323.28
- Grossed back up over 5 years: £1,323.28 x 5 = £6,616.40
So on a preliminary basis I'd estimate tax due on the gain in the region of £6,600-£6,900, but I want to be clear this is indicative only. To confirm it precisely you need to:
- Obtain the formal Chargeable Event Certificate from Momentum, confirming the actual gain, the exact number of relevant years and the encashment date
2. Responding to HMRC
The letter isn't a tax bill - it's a Certificate of Tax Position, issued because HMRC has received information from Guernsey (under international tax information sharing agreements) showing interest and the Momentum proceeds. They're asking you to confirm whether this has already been correctly reported.
Specifically, the information HMRC holds shows:
- Interest from FirstRand Bank Guernsey: £86.85 (2023) and £2.61 (2024)
- Interest from Momentum Wealth International: £1,309.16 (2024)
- Gross proceeds from Momentum Wealth International: £146,540.98 (2024)
What you need to do:
1. Check whether this interest and the bond gain were already reported on a tax return for the relevant years. If you don't normally complete a self-assessment return, or this hasn't previously been declared, it's likely not yet been reported.
2. Complete and return the enclosed Certificate of Tax Position by 3 September 2026, ticking whichever box reflects your circumstances - most likely Box 1 (bringing your tax affairs up to date via HMRC's Worldwide Disclosure Facility) if the gain hasn't already been declared, or Box 2 if it has.
If you require any further information, then please do let me know.
Best wishes,
Jim

Subject: Santander Pension - Retirement Options and Reinvestment Plan
Dear Fiona,
Thank you for sending over the Santander pack and for setting out your thinking. I have reviewed the illustration and your proposed plan in detail, and I am pleased to confirm it stacks up well.
To summarise what you are proposing:
You take Option 2 from the Santander illustration: a tax-free lump sum of £26,801.98, plus a reduced pension of £4,020.30 per year, from your retirement date of 1 December 2026.
The £4,020.30 pension is taxable. As a higher rate taxpayer, the tax due on it is £1,608.12 (40%). Depending on how Gallagher operate PAYE on the payment, you may see basic rate (20%) deducted at source, with the balance collected later via your self-assessment return, or the full 40% deducted straight away. 
You then reinvest the net pension income into your existing Transact pension plan as a personal contribution. Because this goes into a pension rather than a general account, it attracts tax relief in the normal way:
- Your provider adds basic rate relief automatically, grossing your net contribution back up to £4,020.30 in the pension.
- As a higher rate taxpayer, you can also reclaim the further higher rate relief through your self-assessment return, worth £804.06.
The effect of this is that the higher rate tax you pay on receiving the pension, and the higher rate relief you reclaim on reinvesting it, cancel each other out on the same tax return. You end up moving the full £4,020.30 gross amount into your pension each year with no net tax cost, and it stays within a tax-advantaged wrapper rather than sitting in cash or a taxable account.
A couple of points to note for the file and for your peace of mind:
Your income including this pension will sit at around £96,000, which keeps you comfortably under the £100,000 threshold where the personal allowance starts to taper away. Worth keeping an eye on this each year if your earnings move.
The lump sum recycling rules that Gallagher mention in their pack relate specifically to reinvesting tax-free cash, not taxable pension income, so this plan is not caught by that restriction.
Overall, I am comfortable this is a sound and tax efficient way to handle the pension, provided you are happy with the modest annual admin of making the contribution and claiming the additional relief each year through self-assessment.
Could you let me know if you would like me to set up the ongoing contribution instruction into your Transact pension and confirm whether you would like the £26,801.98 lump sum also directed into an investment.
Best wishes,
Jim

Subject: Re: Mortgage Quote – Why This Strategy Works
Hi Tom,
Thank you for the question – it's exactly the right one to ask before committing, and I'm glad you're thinking it through carefully.
Your instinct is right: £15,000 a year in interest with no debt reduction sounds counterintuitive. So let me explain clearly why the numbers still work strongly in your favour.
THE PROBLEM WE'RE SOLVING
At the moment, you're caught in a cycle that looks like this:
  1. You need cash to pay your personal tax bill
  2. To get that cash, you extract dividends from Teacherhead Consulting
  3. Those dividends are themselves taxable income
  4. Which creates a further tax bill the following year
  5. Which requires more dividends… and so it continues
This means you're effectively paying tax on tax – using taxable money to fund a tax liability, which then generates more tax. The cycle is self-perpetuating and expensive.
WHAT THE MORTGAGE DOES
By borrowing £240,000 against your home, you access cash that has no tax consequence whatsoever. It's not income. It doesn't go through the company. It doesn't trigger a dividend tax charge.
This breaks the cycle immediately and permanently.
But there's a second benefit that's equally important: because you no longer need to extract large dividends from the company to fund your tax bills, that money stays inside Teacherhead Consulting. We can then use those retained company profits to make substantial employer pension contributions on your behalf.
Employer pension contributions receive full corporation tax relief – currently 25p in every £1 contributed. And once inside the pension, the money grows free of income tax and capital gains tax.
THE NUMBERS IN SIMPLE TERMS
Mortgage interest cost: approximately £14,400 per year (the £1,202.62 monthly payment)
What you get in return:
  • You avoid dividend tax on each extraction. Additional rate taxpayers pay 39.35% on dividends above the threshold. On large extractions to fund tax bills, this is a significant annual saving.
  • Corporation tax relief on pension contributions. On a £60,000 annual employer contribution (your standard annual allowance going forward), the company saves approximately £15,000 in corporation tax.
  • Pension growth on a significantly larger invested pot, compounding over time, sheltered from all taxes.
In Year One – using carry-forward to make a larger initial contribution – the corporation tax saving alone is likely to exceed the mortgage interest cost. In subsequent years, the two broadly offset, while the pension continues to grow.
WHY INTEREST-ONLY MAKES SENSE HERE
You're not paying down the debt because that's not the purpose of this loan. The mortgage is a tax-efficient mechanism for breaking the dividend cycle, not a conventional home loan. The 10% overpayment facility gives you flexibility if you want to reduce it in future, but there's no obligation to do so.
The loan sits against a property valued at £1,700,000. The £240,000 represents a loan-to-value of approximately 14% – a very conservative position.
IN SHORT
You're spending approximately £14,400 per year in mortgage interest to:
  1. Stop paying tax on tax (saving dividend tax on extractions that no longer need to happen)
  2. Enable significant pension funding with full corporation tax relief
  3. Build a growing, tax-sheltered retirement pot
The interest cost is the price of access to a much more efficient financial structure. For most people in your position, the combined saving comfortably exceeds that cost – often by a meaningful margin.
I'm happy to go through specific projected figures with you or arrange a call if that would help you feel confident before proceeding.

Subject: Re: Mortgage Quote – Why This Strategy Works
Hi Tom,
Thank you for the question – it's exactly the right one to ask before committing, and I'm glad you're thinking it through carefully.
Your instinct is right: £15,000 a year in interest with no debt reduction sounds counterintuitive. So let me explain clearly why the numbers still work strongly in your favour.
THE PROBLEM WE'RE SOLVING
At the moment, you're caught in a cycle that looks like this:
  1. You need cash to pay your personal tax bill
  2. To get that cash, you extract dividends from Teacherhead Consulting
  3. Those dividends are themselves taxable income
  4. Which creates a further tax bill the following year
  5. Which requires more dividends… and so it continues
This means you're effectively paying tax on tax – using taxable money to fund a tax liability, which then generates more tax. The cycle is self-perpetuating and expensive.
WHAT THE MORTGAGE DOES
By borrowing £240,000 against your home, you access cash that has no tax consequence whatsoever. It's not income. It doesn't go through the company. It doesn't trigger a dividend tax charge.
This breaks the cycle immediately and permanently.
But there's a second benefit that's equally important: because you no longer need to extract large dividends from the company to fund your tax bills, that money stays inside Teacherhead Consulting. We can then use those retained company profits to make substantial employer pension contributions on your behalf.
Employer pension contributions receive full corporation tax relief – currently 25p in every £1 contributed. And once inside the pension, the money grows free of income tax and capital gains tax.
THE NUMBERS IN SIMPLE TERMS
Mortgage interest cost: approximately £14,400 per year (the £1,202.62 monthly payment)
What you get in return:
  • You avoid dividend tax on each extraction. Additional rate taxpayers pay 39.35% on dividends above the threshold. On large extractions to fund tax bills, this is a significant annual saving.
  • Corporation tax relief on pension contributions. On a £60,000 annual employer contribution (your standard annual allowance going forward), the company saves approximately £15,000 in corporation tax.
  • Pension growth on a significantly larger invested pot, compounding over time, sheltered from all taxes.
In Year One – using carry-forward to make a larger initial contribution – the corporation tax saving alone is likely to exceed the mortgage interest cost. In subsequent years, the two broadly offset, while the pension continues to grow.
WHY INTEREST-ONLY MAKES SENSE HERE
You're not paying down the debt because that's not the purpose of this loan. The mortgage is a tax-efficient mechanism for breaking the dividend cycle, not a conventional home loan. The 10% overpayment facility gives you flexibility if you want to reduce it in future, but there's no obligation to do so.
The loan sits against a property valued at £1,700,000. The £240,000 represents a loan-to-value of approximately 14% – a very conservative position.
IN SHORT
You're spending approximately £14,400 per year in mortgage interest to:
  1. Stop paying tax on tax (saving dividend tax on extractions that no longer need to happen)
  2. Enable significant pension funding with full corporation tax relief
  3. Build a growing, tax-sheltered retirement pot
The interest cost is the price of access to a much more efficient financial structure. For most people in your position, the combined saving comfortably exceeds that cost – often by a meaningful margin.

Subject: Re: Your tax funding strategy — mortgage vs dividends
Hi Tom,
Good to hear from you, and it's a fair question. Let me set out clearly what the mortgage is actually doing for you, because there are two separate benefits at work and it's easy to run them together.
The short version: the mortgage interest is the cost. Against it sit two benefits — (1) the dividend tax you no longer must pay just to get hold of the cash, and (2) the company profit you free up, which can then grow in your pension. Both comfortably outweigh the interest. It isn't strictly the borrowed money going into the pension — more on that below.
A worked example (illustrative figures while we wait on Brian)
Take a £100,000 tax payment.
Paying it from dividends: at your level dividends are taxed at 39.35%, so to end up with £100,000 in hand you'd have to draw roughly £165,000 gross. That's about £65,000 of tax just to access £100,000 — and that £165,000 dividend then inflates next year's bill and your payments on account, which is exactly the cycle we're trying to break.
Paying it by borrowing: you borrow £100,000 and the cost is interest only — around £5,500 a year at an assumed 5.5%. So, in year one you're weighing roughly £65,000 of tax against roughly £5,500 of interest. Even if you held that borrowing in place for more than a decade, the interest still wouldn't add up to the tax you'd have paid in a single year — and you've stopped feeding the cycle.
That's the first benefit, and it's the main event.
The second benefit is the pension. Because you're no longer pulling £165,000 out as a dividend, that profit stays in the company and can be paid into your pension as an employer contribution. It goes in with full corporation tax relief (a 25% saving), grows free of income and capital gains tax, and — because your defined benefit pension is in draw rather than accrual — doesn't use up your annual allowance. On the growth rate we've been working with, a contribution of that size would be expected to roughly double inside about seven years, well ahead of a 5.5% mortgage. (That growth is an assumption for illustration, not a promise — investments can fall as well as rise.)
So, to your specific question: yes, the "grows faster than the interest" idea is part of it — but to be precise, it isn't the borrowed money going into the pension. The borrowing pays your tax; the profit you've kept in the company by not extracting it is what funds the pension.
On the "forever mortgage": I completely understand, and the plan doesn't rely on you keeping it indefinitely. The mortgage is a bridge to break the cycle. Once your dividends are down at the ~£80,000 level and the pension is building, future tax bills are far smaller and manageable from income — at which point you can repay on whatever timescale suits you, whether from surplus income or from your pension tax-free cash later. The only thing I'd flag is a modest inheritance-tax advantage to carrying some debt (the outstanding balance comes off your taxable estate, so roughly 40% of it), so there's no rush to clear it purely for its own sake. But being debt-free is a perfectly sensible goal and we'll plan around it — entirely your call.
On the timing — money sitting idle until January: good catch, and there are two clean ways to handle it. The neatest is to arrange the borrowing as an offset facility, so the money you've drawn but not yet spent sits against the loan and you pay no net interest on it until you need it for the January payment. If the product is instead a single advance at completion, we simply park the portion earmarked for January in a competitive instant-access account or money market fund — the interest there offsets most of the borrowing cost for those few months, so holding it early costs you very little. We'll check the flexibility of the specific product when we get to the mortgage stage.
Brian — when you have a moment, the figures we still need are the revised personal tax position at the lower dividend level, confirmation there were no money-purchase pension contributions in the relevant carry-forward years, and the company's cash position after corporation tax. Once those are in, I'll firm up the numbers above so Tom can see his actual position rather than the illustration.
Happy to jump on a call if it's easier to talk it through.
Kind regards,
Jim

Hi Tom,
Good to hear from you, and it's a fair question. Let me set out clearly what the mortgage is actually doing for you, because there are two separate benefits at work and it's easy to run them together.
The short version: the mortgage interest is the cost. Against it sit two benefits — (1) the dividend tax you no longer must pay just to get hold of the cash, and (2) the company profit you free up, which can then grow in your pension. Both comfortably outweigh the interest. It isn't strictly the borrowed money going into the pension — more on that below.
A worked example (illustrative figures while we wait on Brian)
Take a £100,000 tax payment.
Paying it from dividends: at your level dividends are taxed at 39.35%, so to end up with £100,000 in hand you'd have to draw roughly £165,000 gross. That's about £65,000 of tax just to access £100,000 — and that £165,000 dividend then inflates next year's bill and your payments on account, which is exactly the cycle we're trying to break.
Paying it by borrowing: you borrow £100,000 and the cost is interest only — around £5,500 a year at an assumed 5.5%. So, in year one you're weighing roughly £65,000 of tax against roughly £5,500 of interest. Even if you held that borrowing in place for more than a decade, the interest still wouldn't add up to the tax you'd have paid in a single year — and you've stopped feeding the cycle.
That's the first benefit, and it's the main event.
The second benefit is the pension. Because you're no longer pulling £165,000 out as a dividend, that profit stays in the company and can be paid into your pension as an employer contribution. It goes in with full corporation tax relief (a 25% saving), grows free of income and capital gains tax, and — because your defined benefit pension is in draw rather than accrual — doesn't use up your annual allowance. On the growth rate we've been working with, a contribution of that size would be expected to roughly double inside about seven years, well ahead of a 5.5% mortgage. (That growth is an assumption for illustration, not a promise — investments can fall as well as rise.)
So, to your specific question: yes, the "grows faster than the interest" idea is part of it — but to be precise, it isn't the borrowed money going into the pension. The borrowing pays your tax; the profit you've kept in the company by not extracting it is what funds the pension.
On the "forever mortgage": I completely understand, and the plan doesn't rely on you keeping it indefinitely. The mortgage is a bridge to break the cycle. Once your dividends are down at the ~£80,000 level and the pension is building, future tax bills are far smaller and manageable from income — at which point you can repay on whatever timescale suits you, whether from surplus income or from your pension tax-free cash later. The only thing I'd flag is a modest inheritance-tax advantage to carrying some debt (the outstanding balance comes off your taxable estate, so roughly 40% of it), so there's no rush to clear it purely for its own sake. But being debt-free is a perfectly sensible goal and we'll plan around it — entirely your call.
On the timing — money sitting idle until January: good catch, and there are two clean ways to handle it. The neatest is to arrange the borrowing as an offset facility, so the money you've drawn but not yet spent sits against the loan and you pay no net interest on it until you need it for the January payment. If the product is instead a single advance at completion, we simply park the portion earmarked for January in a competitive instant-access account or money market fund — the interest there offsets most of the borrowing cost for those few months, so holding it early costs you very little. We'll check the flexibility of the specific product when we get to the mortgage stage.
Brian — when you have a moment, the figures we still need are the revised personal tax position at the lower dividend level, confirmation there were no money-purchase pension contributions in the relevant carry-forward years, and the company's cash position after corporation tax. Once those are in, I'll firm up the numbers above so Tom can see his actual position rather than the illustration.
Happy to jump on a call if it's easier to talk it through.
Kind regards,
Jim

THE PROPOSED SOLUTION: JOINT LIFE 2ND DEATH POLICY
A joint life 2nd death policy is specifically designed for married couples and pays out on the death of the surviving spouse. This makes it the ideal product for your situation.
The positive news is that both of you will be covered under the same policy. Mahmood, you have been fully assessed by Zurich, and they are satisfied that your health profile is acceptable within this type of policy structure. Because a joint life 2nd death policy only pays out when the second person passes away, your health conditions do not adversely affect the insurer's risk in the way they would under a standalone policy. This is why Zurich are able to include you — and importantly, why the premium remains very competitive.
The premium will be calculated based on Shamin's health alone, which means you will not face any additional loading as a result of your medical history, Mahmood. That is a genuinely good outcome for you both.
WHY THIS IS THE RIGHT STRUCTURE FOR YOUR ESTATE
The reason a joint life 2nd death policy is so well suited to your needs comes down to how inheritance tax works for married couples. When the first spouse passes away, assets can pass to the surviving spouse entirely free of inheritance tax, thanks to the spouse exemption. Subject: RE: Vanguard U.S. Equity Index — CGT Cost Basis
Dear Chris,
Thank you for the screenshot and for flagging the reinvested dividends point — you are absolutely right to raise it, and it is an important distinction.
For accumulation funds, the platform only records the cash you physically invested. However, because accumulation units roll income back into the unit price rather than paying it out, HMRC treats that income as having been received and taxed each year (it appears on your annual tax certificates as accumulated or reported income). Since you have already paid income tax on those amounts, they are added to your CGT cost basis — otherwise you would effectively be taxed twice on the same money.
Your adjusted cost basis is therefore:
Platform book cost + Cumulative reported income attributed to your units over the holding period
The good news is that for a partial transfer, the purchase dates of individual units are not relevant. HMRC pools all units of the same fund together (a Section 104 pool), so once we have the total adjusted cost, we simply apply the proportion of units being transferred:
Allowable cost = (Units transferred ÷ Total units held) × Total adjusted pool cost
In terms of reconstructing the reported income figures, the best sources are:
1. Your annual consolidated tax certificates from Interactive Investor — these should show accumulated income year by year.
2. Vanguard's published historical reported income per unit, available on their website by fund ISIN.
3. If either of these proves difficult to access, Vanguard's investor relations team can usually provide the data on request.
Given the scale of the gain involved, if a full reconstruction proves impractical, it would be worth engaging a tax accountant to do this properly — the cost would be modest relative to the tax at stake, and it protects you if HMRC ever queries the calculation.
As discussed, the Section 260 holdover relief election will be an important part of the trust transfer process, and I will ensure Paul Colman has everything he needs on that front before we proceed.
Please do let me know once you have a clearer idea of the number of units you are looking to transfer and we can work through the numbers from there.

Dear Chris,
Thank you so much for getting back to me – and please don't worry about the delay at all. This is excellent news and I'm delighted you're happy to proceed.
Let me work through your points and questions in turn.
Confirmed instructions
To summarise what we're putting in place:
- FIC with an initial investment of approximately £1 million
- All three trust structures
- Whole of Life cover
I'll begin co-ordinating with Paul on the legal documentation and come back to you with a clear timeline and checklist of what we'll need from you to get everything moving.
On the GIVOS policies
I'd gently encourage you to reconsider keeping these in place, and here's why I think they remain an important part of the plan.
The Whole of Life policy is excellent for covering the long-term IHT liability, but the GIVOS (Gift Inter Vivos) policies serve a very specific and different purpose — they are designed to cover the tapering IHT liability on the gifts you are making into the trusts during the seven-year period following each gift. If either of you were to die within those seven years, the trusts would not yet be fully outside your estate for IHT purposes, and HMRC would look to the trustees or beneficiaries for the tax due. The GIVOS policies cover exactly that risk, reducing on a tapered basis in line with the reducing IHT exposure as each year passes.
Given that you are proceeding with all three trust structures — each involving a chargeable transfer — you will have multiple seven-year windows running concurrently. The GIVOS policies are the clean, low-cost solution to covering that bridging risk, and as you noted yourself, the premiums are relatively modest. They also sit in trust, so the pay-out would be outside your estate and available immediately to meet any liability without delay or probate.
In the context of the overall planning, you are putting in place, it would be a shame to leave this specific risk uncovered when the cost of doing so is so small. I would recommend we proceed with the applications alongside everything else.
Your questions
On the mortgage and IHT
You are right to question this – your instinct is correct. On day one, if you borrow £1 million against the property and lend that amount to the FIC, your net estate position is indeed unchanged. The mortgage liability is offset by the loan receivable from the FIC, so there is no immediate IHT saving.
The benefit is more indirect and accumulates over time in two ways:
First, growth outside your estate. The FIC invests and grows the £1 million, but that growth belongs to the FIC shareholders – typically the next generation – not to you. Your loan receivable stays fixed at £1 million regardless of how well the investments perform, so all future uplift happens entirely outside your estate. Over time, this differential can be very material.
Second, the mortgage interest itself drains your estate. On an interest-only mortgage of £1 million you might be paying in the region of £40,000–£50,000 per year. That money leaves your estate each year as ordinary expenditure with no IHT consequences. Over seven-plus years that alone could amount to £280,000–£350,000 of estate reduction. There is also the possibility that the interest may be deductible against your income tax, which would reduce the effective out-of-pocket cost.
Finally, if at some future point you chose to write off the loan to the FIC rather than seek repayment, that would constitute a gift and start the seven-year IHT clock on that amount.
In short – it is not an immediate estate reducer, but a mechanism for gradually draining the estate through interest payments while ensuring all investment growth occurs outside it. Paul will ensure the loan arrangement and any future forgiveness are properly documented.
On the CGT holdover trusts and the FIC
Yes – to confirm absolutely. The two discretionary trusts (into which the shares were gifted using CGT holdover relief) are separate legal structures from the FIC. They are independent trusts with their own trustees, their own assets, and their own ongoing compliance requirements. The FIC is a private limited company. The two sit alongside each other as complementary parts of your overall estate plan but do not interact unless you were to specifically direct them to do so.
Please do give me a call if you'd like to talk through any of this, and I'll be in touch shortly with next steps.

We agreed to stay the course and not attempt to time the market around geopolitical events.
- Mortgage Strategy: Your current mortgage deal expires at the end of May. We discussed your plan to remortgage to an interest-only basis on a total of £310,000, which would keep your monthly payments at approximately £900–£1,000. Please forward me your self-assessment tax returns for the last three years, along with your TFL pension contribution figures, and I will work through the numbers and come back to you with a clear explanation.
- Inheritance Tax Planning: We touched on the anticipated changes from April 2027, when pensions may be brought into an individual's estate for IHT purposes. We discussed the importance of starting to draw down pensions more actively at that stage rather than letting them accumulate further, taking tax-free cash and potentially moving funds into a more IHT-efficient vehicle. We also noted that maintaining mortgage debt is itself a useful IHT strategy, as it reduces the net estate value.
- Lasting Powers of Attorney: We made good progress on signing the LPA documents today. The remaining pages need to be completed at home and posted in advance of the deadline. Please do prioritise getting these finished — as we discussed, the importance of having these in place cannot be overstated.
- Fee Increase: I wanted to flag that we are making a small increase to our adviser fee, from 0.6% to 0.7% per annum. This equates to approximately £50 per month for you. It is not something I have done lightly — this is the first increase since we started working together. As a reminder, all performance figures I share with you are quoted net of all fees.
Next Steps:
1. Mortgage Introduction: I will introduce you to David Conway to explore the remortgage options, including moving to interest-only on £310,000, and adding Cath to the mortgage and property title.
2. Pension Tax Relief: Please forward your self-assessment tax returns for the last three years along with your TFL pension contribution figures. I will review these and provide a clear breakdown of the tax relief position.

5. Risk Profile: I will write to you to formally confirm your attitude to risk has not changed before issuing our annual review letter.

When someone earns over £100,000 in the UK, they face a particularly punitive effective marginal tax rate due to the loss of their personal allowance. Here's how pension contributions help:
The Problem
Once your income exceeds £100,000, you lose £1 of personal allowance for every £2 earned above this threshold. The personal allowance (£12,570 for 2024/25) is completely eliminated by £125,140.
This creates an effective marginal tax rate of 60% on income between £100,000 and £125,140:

You pay 40% income tax on the extra income
Plus you lose personal allowance worth 40% tax relief on another £1 for every £2 earned
Combined effect: 40% + (40% × 50%) = 60%

How Pension Contributions Help
Making pension contributions reduces your adjusted net income - the figure used to determine personal allowance entitlement.
Example
Say you earn £120,000:

Without pension contribution: Personal allowance reduced to £2,570 (lost £10,000 of it)
Make £20,000 gross pension contribution
Adjusted net income becomes £100,000
You retain your full £12,570 personal allowance

The Tax Savings
On that £20,000 contribution, you effectively get:

Basic 20% tax relief automatically (grossed up contribution)
Additional 20% higher rate relief via self-assessment
Plus you've saved 40% tax on the £10,000 of personal allowance you preserved
Total effective relief: 60% on the portion that brings you back below £100,000

This makes pension contributions exceptionally tax-efficient for anyone in the £100,000-£125,140 bracket - you're getting 60p of tax relief for every pound contributed (on the portion reducing income back towards £100,000).

For a client earning £114,000, the optimal pension contribution is £14,000 (gross).
Why This Amount?
This brings their adjusted net income down to exactly £100,000, which:

Restores their full personal allowance of £12,570
Eliminates the punitive 60% marginal rate entirely
Maximizes the tax efficiency of the contribution

The Tax Relief Breakdown
On a £14,000 gross contribution:

£2,800 basic rate relief (20%) - added automatically to pension
£2,800 higher rate relief (additional 20%) - claimed via self-assessment
£5,028 saved by preserving personal allowance (40% × £12,570)
Total tax saving: £10,628

This represents effective tax relief of 76% on the net cost to your client.
Net Cost to Client

Gross contribution: £14,000
Less total tax relief: £10,628
Net cost: £3,372

So for £3,372 out of pocket, they get £14,000 into their pension.
Practical Considerations

Ensure they have sufficient annual allowance (£60,000 standard, potentially plus carry forward)
Check if employer can facilitate via salary sacrifice for additional NI savings
If self-employed, they'll make the net contribution (£11,200) and claim full relief via tax return
Consider cash flow - they may prefer to spread contributions across the tax year

Does your client have any carry-forward allowance available that might allow for a larger contribution?

Dear Sue,
I'm sorry to hear about your own health challenges and hope your treatment goes well.
Thank you for reaching out to Kelly. I understand she's responded and is willing to give her father a call, though understandably concerned about what she can do if he won't admit he needs help.
Could you please pass on the following information to Kelly? It's important she understands there are legal mechanisms available even if her father won't cooperate.
Key message for Kelly:
Regarding your father's situation - you don't need his permission or cooperation to protect him if he lacks capacity due to dementia and is being exploited. This is precisely what the legal system's safeguarding mechanisms exist for.
Immediate steps you should take:

 Contact a solicitor specializing in Court of Protection      work -      They can advise on applying for a Deputyship Order, which would give you      legal authority to manage his affairs and protect him, even if he objects      or doesn't recognize the need.
 Report the suspected financial exploitation to: 
 
  Adult Social Services (safeguarding team) -       they have a statutory duty to investigate suspected financial abuse of       vulnerable adults
  The Office of the       Public Guardian
      - they can investigate and take action
  His bank - they can flag the       account and monitor for suspicious transactions
  Police if you believe       criminal exploitation is occurring
 
 Arrange a capacity assessment - Ask his GP to conduct      a formal assessment of whether he has mental capacity to make financial      decisions. This will be crucial evidence for any legal proceedings.
 Gather evidence - If possible, try to obtain bank statements or      documentation of any unusual financial transactions or suspicious      activity.

Important to understand:

 The Court of Protection exists specifically for      situations where someone lacks capacity and needs protection, even against      their own wishes
 Adult Social Services have a legal duty to investigate      when vulnerable adults are at risk
 Estrangement doesn't remove your legal standing - as      his only child, you have both the right and arguably a responsibility to      act when he's vulnerable
 Time is critical - the longer any exploitation continues, the greater      the financial and emotional harm

The phone call is a good start but given the concerns about his capacity and potential exploitation, legal intervention may be necessary regardless of how that conversation goes.
I would strongly encourage getting legal advice, if possible, given the urgency of the situation.
Sue, I hope this information is helpful. Please feel free to share it with Kelly in whatever way seems most appropriate.
If you need any clarification on any of these points, please don't hesitate to contact me.
Best wishes,
Jim

[task note by Jim Hoban on 2025-12-03 "Transact Withdrawal Form"]
this is a question about top slicing of a UK onshore bond.  My client is a basic rate tax payer and is encashing £10k from his bond.  Please explain the following:     
Good morning,
 
Thank you for the recent bond withdrawal instruction however, a withdrawal for £10,000 taken proportionately across all segments would trigger a chargeable gain of £7,180. Please note that future adviser fees in the current policy year would increase the gain.
 
Alternatively, the same amount could be withdrawn by surrendering 4 segments with a small proportional withdrawal. There would be a gain of approx. £1,940 on the segments.
 
Please confirm how to proceed.
Show more
This is about managing the tax efficiency of the withdrawal. Let me break down what's happening:
The two options differ in how the gain arises:
Option 1 - Proportionate withdrawal across all segments:

Takes £10,000 proportionately from all segments
Creates a chargeable gain of £7,180
This means £7,180 of the £10,000 withdrawn represents growth (the rest is return of capital)

Option 2 - Surrender 4 whole segments plus small top-up:

Fully surrenders 4 segments, then takes a small amount from remaining segments
Creates a gain of only £1,940
Much more tax efficient

Why the difference?
The segments being surrendered in Option 2 likely have relatively little growth compared to the overall policy average. By carefully selecting which segments to surrender, you're crystallising less gain for the same gross withdrawal.
Top slicing relief:
Since your client is a basic rate taxpayer, top slicing becomes important. The chargeable gain is divided by the number of complete policy years to get the "slice." This slice is added to their income to see if it pushes them into higher rate tax.
With a £7,180 gain, the slice could push them into 40% tax on some or all of the gain. With a £1,940 gain, they're much more likely to stay within basic rate, meaning no additional tax liability (as the 20% tax credit within the bond covers basic rate liability).
My recommendation:
Go with Option 2 - surrender the 4 segments. It's significantly more tax efficient and keeps your client's liability minimal or nil.

[case note by Jim Hoban on 2025-11-15 "Onboarding"]
1. Capital Gains Tax on Share Transfer


You are completely correct. The transfer of shares to his daughter, regardless of how it's structured, will be treated as a disposal for CGT purposes under TCGA 1992 s.17.
Critical points:

This is a connected persons transaction (father-daughter relationship)
Under TCGA 1992 s.18, the disposal is deemed to occur at market value regardless of actual consideration
Even if structured as a "sale" for a loan note, CGT is triggered on the market value of the shares
If he tries to sell at undervalue, HMRC will substitute market value anyway
The CGT charge arises immediately upon transfer, not when/if the loan note is paid

2. The IHT "Avoidance" - The Fatal Flaw
You are absolutely right to be skeptical. This arrangement does NOT avoid IHT, and the advice appears fundamentally flawed.
Why the loan note doesn't solve the IHT problem:
The loan note is itself an asset in his estate. Under IHTA 1984 s.5, his estate includes all property to which he is beneficially entitled - this includes debts owed to him.
Three scenarios, all problematic:


He writes off the loan note during his lifetime:

This is a transfer of value (IHTA 1984 s.3)
It's a Potentially Exempt Transfer (PET)
If he dies within 7 years, it's added back into his estate for IHT
This is exactly what IHT legislation is designed to catch



He writes it off in his Will:

The loan note is an estate asset at death
Valued at full amount and subject to 40% IHT

[task note by Jim Hoban on 2025-09-29 "Clarify inheritance tax rules for Hadley Enterprises SSAS scheme"]
This significantly complicates the death benefit situation and strengthens your case for the Whole of Life policy even further.
The Reality of Your Client's Position
With two other members and the property actively used by the commercial business, here's what would realistically happen on your client's death:
The Dilemma Facing the Trustees
The SSAS trustees (which likely include your client and the other members) would face conflicting duties:

Legal obligation: Pay death benefits of £500,000 to your client's beneficiaries
Practical reality: The business needs the property to continue operating
Other members' interests: The two surviving members need the SSAS to retain the property for their own pension benefits

Likely Scenarios
Scenario 1: The Other Members Must Buy Out the Deceased's Share

The two surviving members would need to find £500,000 (personally or through the business) to effectively "buy out" your client's share
This could be achieved by:

Personal funds (if available)
Business profits
External borrowing
The SSAS taking a loan (up to 50% of scheme value)


This creates significant financial pressure on the surviving members and potentially the business

Scenario 2: Forced Property Sale

If liquidity can't be arranged, the property must be sold
This would:

Disrupt the business operations
Force the two surviving members to find new pension investment vehicles
Potentially occur at an unfavorable time/price
Take time (commercial property sales aren't quick)



Scenario 3: Beneficiary Drawdown with Extended Timeline

Your client's beneficiaries take their inheritance via drawdown over many years
The property remains in the SSAS
Death benefits are paid gradually from rental income or business rent payments
However:

This delays inheritance significantly
May not suit beneficiaries' needs
Could create tension between beneficiaries and surviving members
Still requires the business to generate sufficient rental income



The Two-Year Tax-Free Window Problem
Remember: if your client dies before age 75, the £500,000 should be tax-free to beneficiaries only if paid within two years of notification of death.

Selling a commercial property with sitting tenants typically takes 6-12+ months
Arranging financing for the other members takes time
If it takes longer than two years, that £500,000 becomes taxable at the beneficiaries' marginal rates
This could mean £200,000 or more in unnecessary tax on what should have been a tax-free pension death benefit

The Commercial Property Valuation Issue
Another critical point:

Your client's member account shows £500,000, but is this based on a recent professional valuation of the property?
Commercial property values can fluctuate significantly
If the property has increased in value, their share might actually be worth more (increasing the liquidity problem)
If it's decreased, there could be disputes about valuation when death benefits are calculated

Why This Strengthens the Case for Whole of Life Cover
This situation makes the £1million Whole of Life policy even more critical:
It Solves Multiple Problems

Provides liquidity for IHT: The original £800,000 IHT liability is covered
Provides liquidity for SSAS buy-out: The policy proceeds could enable the family/beneficiaries to be patient about the SSAS payout
Protects the business: The business isn't forced to find £500,000 immediately
Protects the other members: They have time to arrange financing without crisis pressure
Protects beneficiaries: They receive immediate funds and can afford to wait for the SSAS to be properly resolved
Preserves tax efficiency: With liquid funds available, there's less pressure to breach the two-year window

The Real Risk Profile
Without the protection policy, your client's death creates a cascade of financial problems:

£800,000 IHT bill due within 6 months
£500,000 locked in an illiquid SSAS
Business disruption or forced member buy-out
Potential loss of tax-free status on pension benefits
Family forced to sell other assets in a hurry
Surviving business partners facing financial strain

A Strengthened Email Addition
You might consider adding a paragraph to your email specifically addressing this:
A Further Consideration – Your SSAS
I should also mention that your £500,000 SSAS member account, while outside your estate for IHT purposes, presents its own liquidity challenge given that the underlying asset is the commercial property used by the business. On your death, the trustees would need to find £500,000 to pay death benefits to your beneficiaries, but the property needs to remain operational for the business and the two other members. This would likely mean the other members needing to buy out your share, or your beneficiaries having to wait for the property to be sold or take drawdown over an extended period. The Whole of Life policy would have provided immediate liquidity to your family, allowing the SSAS situation to be resolved properly without forcing rushed decisions or putting undue pressure on your business partners.
Questions to Consider


What's the current professional valuation of the property? Is £500,000 still accurate for your client's one-third share?


What's the succession plan for the business? Who would take over your client's role?


Do the other two members have adequate liquidity to buy out your client's share on death?


Is there a formal agreement between the three members about what happens on death?


Have the other members considered protection for themselves given the same issues apply to them?


This is actually a much more complex estate planning situation than a straightforward IHT problem. The interconnection between the business, the SSAS property, the other members, and the estate creates significant risk that the Whole of Life policy was specifically designed to mitigate.

Dear Ian & Jane,
Further to our telephone conversation today. I wanted to follow up on our discussion about your Whole of Life insurance quote and address some of the concerns you raised about proceeding with the £1,000,000 sum assured at £1,445 per month.
I completely understand that this feels like a significant financial commitment, and it's natural to want to carefully consider all aspects before deciding. However, I'd like to help you see this policy from a different perspective that might make the benefits clearer.
Think of This as Your Family's Guaranteed Savings Plan
Rather than viewing this as just another insurance policy, I'd encourage you to think of it as a guaranteed savings plan specifically designed to protect your family's inheritance. Every month, you're essentially putting aside £1,445 into a plan that guarantees your beneficiaries will receive exactly £1,000,000 when they need it most - completely free from the uncertainty that comes with traditional investments or market fluctuations.
The reality is that inheritance tax could take up to  £1,000,000 from your estate. This policy ensures that full amount is protected, meaning your family receives everything you've worked so hard to build, rather than losing this substantial sum to HMRC.
Time Is Working Against Us
Here's what I need to stress: your current quote is only valid until 23rd September. This isn't just an arbitrary deadline - it represents a window of opportunity that may not reopen on the same terms.
If you decide to revisit this decision in six months or a year's time, several things will have changed. First, you'll be older, and premiums increase significantly with each passing year - we could be looking at hundreds of pounds more annually. More importantly, your health assessment will need to be completely redone. The standard rates you've been offered today are based on your current health status, which we simply cannot guarantee will remain unchanged.
I've seen too many clients who thought they could "just get cover later" only to find that a minor health issue - perhaps something as routine as elevated blood pressure or cholesterol - resulted in significantly higher premiums or, in some cases, declined coverage altogether.
Flexibility Within Your Comfort Zone
I also want you to know that if £1,000,000 feels overwhelming right now, we can absolutely explore a lower sum assured that fits more comfortably within your budget. The key is securing your health rating and establishing the policy now, while you have the option to do so at standard rates.
Starting with a lower amount still provides valuable protection for your family, and many clients find it easier to gradually increase their comfort level with the premiums once they see how seamlessly the policy integrates into their financial planning.
The Bottom Line
What we're really talking about here is peace of mind - knowing that regardless of what happens with markets, property values, or tax legislation changes, your family will have exactly what they need to preserve your legacy. This isn't about the insurance company's benefit; it's about ensuring your life's work goes to your loved ones rather than the taxman.
You have until 23rd September to make this decision. After that date, we're essentially starting from scratch with a new application, new medical requirements, and no guarantee of these rates.
I'd be happy to discuss alternative sum assured levels that might feel more comfortable initially. 
Best wishes,
Jim
